newsitem.title: USA: Slain militia member wanted in California - report.
newsitem.headline: Slain militia member wanted in California - report.

text.p: A Republic of Texas militia member believed killed in the west Texas mountains was wanted in California and had vowed to "die fighting" rather than return to jail, the Oakland Tribune reported Tuesday.
Michael Matson and another militiaman fled three days ago when other members of the group surrendered after a standoff with police in Texas.

One of the fugitives was killed Monday after he fired on bloodhounds and police in a helicopter. Police identified the dead militia member as a "middle-aged white man," believed to be Matson, 48, who was wanted for questioning.

The Oakland Tribune said Matson lived in Berkeley and Oakland from 1983 to 1996 and had long complained that he was the victim of a wide-ranging conspiracy by everyone from lawyers and judges to police and the news media.

It said he sent the newspaper a packet of documents in December, including a newsletter article quoting Matson as saying: "I don't intend to survive another jail term. If I am to die, I will die fighting somehow -- somewhere."

It was one of scores of rambling, expletive-riddled letters that Matson sent in the last five years, making wild accusations about the courts in Alameda County in northern California, the Oakland Tribune said.

Chicago-born Matson had been convicted of misdemeanor contempt of court charges in May 1995 in Alameda County Municipal Court. A $250,000 arrest warrant was issued for Matson in March 1996 after he violated his probation by leaving California, the newspaper said.

Matson had been accused of harassing an attorney who represented inheritors of an estate that Matson unsuccessfully laid claim to. He also was being investigated for allegedly making threats to the lawyer and to an Alameda County Municipal Court judge, the Tribune quoted authorities as saying.

Matson spent the last year moving from state to state and apparently wound up a few months ago at the Republic of Texas compound, where he found others who were angry at the government, the Tribune said.
